We combine scientific curiosity, innovation, and the drive to solve real-world agricultural problems. Our purpose is to bring practical solutions to those who work the land, using Earth observation data and accessible tools."
summary:
What did we develop?

We developed Rotaterra, a decision-support web application to organize crop rotation in summer-harvest agricultural systems. It integrates NASA satellite data with an agronomic database of the five dominant crops (soybean, corn, sorghum, sunflower, and peanut), evaluating water requirements, heat stress, water balance, and mandatory sanitary breaks through an algorithm that filters viable options and ranks optimal sequences per plot.

How is it addressed?

We structured the solution around three pillars: optimization of alternation among main crops, a dual interface that provides direct simplicity for the producer and parameter customization for the agronomist, and local adaptability to adjust agronomic thresholds against climate variability.

Why is it important?

In Argentina, these five crops account for over 95% of the agricultural area (and exceed 51% globally). Repeating them without criteria degrades the soil, multiplies resistant weeds, and increases financial risk. Rotaterra democratizes precision agriculture free of charge and without requiring field sensors, mitigating water and climate losses with NASA's scientific backing.
details:
¿What does it do exactly?

It is a decision-support web application that, through a search engine based on clear (and scientifically grounded) agronomic guidelines, recommends rotation sequences among the main summer-harvest crops (Soybean, Corn, Sorghum, Sunflower, and Peanut). Through its interface, the system cross-references NASA satellite sensor data for the plot with the technical requirements of each crop, allowing users to evaluate the viability of each crop and design an alternation scheme that avoids risky repetitions, protects the soil, and optimizes available water.

How does it work?

The platform operates through an intuitive workflow that translates satellite information into practical field recommendations in just three steps. Upon entering, the user is greeted with a welcome screen that allows choosing between two work profiles according to their needs (Figure Nº 1):

Farmer Mode: Specifically designed for producers in regions with climate variability and limited access to precision equipment, who need reliable technical information without complications.

Agricultural Technician Mode: An advanced environment for agronomists that allows customizing thresholds, adjusting parameters, and cross-referencing satellite data with their professional diagnosis for complex planning.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"" ]

Figure N° 1 Web App Login. 

Step-by-step of the main workflow (MVP - Farmer Mode):

Plot delimitation (Figure Nº 2): The web app asks to locate the plot of interest. To facilitate this task without using complex software, the user can define the area by drawing a rectangle of fixed dimensions or marking points on the map to generate the plot automatically.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"" ]

Figure Nº 2 Plot creation. 

Crop history (Figure Nº 3): Once the plot is confirmed, the latest status of the parcel is indicated by selecting the previous crop from five main summer-harvest options (or the "None/Other" option for fallow situations or different crop residues).

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"" ]

Figure Nº 3 Latest status. 

Upon advancing to Stage 3, the application begins the process of querying and processing information. To obtain the results, it is necessary to wait for the connection with the satellite information sources to complete and for RotaTerra's analysis engine to process the obtained data, contrast it with the agronomic requirements of each crop, and apply the previously configured evaluation logic.

Once this process is finished, the platform presents as its main result the recommendation for the next sowing and a crop rotation proposal for the following three years.

In the panels shown in Figure Nº 4, the recommendations generated by RotaTerra based on the previously entered configuration are displayed. To do this, the platform cross-references the characteristics and conditions of the plot, obtained through satellite information, with the agronomic requirements necessary for the development of each crop.

The panels display the recommendation index, the agronomic criteria considered to determine the compatibility of the crop with the plot, and the technical justification for each result. As a reference, the analysis incorporates historical information corresponding to the last 30 agricultural seasons, which allows contextualizing the recommendations based on productive records and conditions registered in previous periods.

On the same screen, a traffic-light system is incorporated to quickly visualize the suitability of the different crops for the analyzed plot. Crops classified as "Optimal" are identified in green; those that present certain restrictions or require particular management conditions are shown in yellow; while crops that present incompatibilities or unfavorable conditions for the plot are identified in red and are discarded as sowing alternatives.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"" ]

Figure Nº 4 Crop recommendation. 

Following these panels, at the bottom of the screen, a series of boxes detail the evaluation of each recommendation and the agronomic criteria considered for its determination, as seen in Figure Nº 5. 

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"" ]

Figure Nº 5 Crop evaluation. 

In the final part of Stage 3, six cards are presented that identify the main parameters obtained through satellite information, showing for each one the latest available data recorded by the satellite (Figure Nº 6). Likewise, each card allows user interaction to access a graphical representation of the parameter's evolution over time, with a query period automatically configured for up to five years of historical information. 

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"" ]

Figure Nº 6 Satellite parameters panel.

Finally, the platform offers the option to export a PDF file with all the processed data and four key charts to evaluate crop yield, as shown in Figure Nº 7.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"" ]

Figure Nº 7 PDF Report.

What benefits does it have?

Today, agriculture does not suffer from a lack of information; it suffers from an excess of noise. The market is full of platforms that provide moisture maps, greenness indices, and scattered forecasts, leaving you alone in front of the screen trying to guess what to do.

Rotaterra puts NASA's space intelligence at the service of your field under an implacable logic: the real agronomy of rotation. Simply by locating your plot, it cross-references satellite data with the demands of summer-harvest crops and delivers a clear plan, providing five concrete advantages:

 Lower costs, better crop health: By respecting sanitary breaks and alternating botanical families, we break the cycles of pests, diseases, and weeds, reducing unnecessary spending on agrochemicals.

 Smart water and soil management: We avoid planting high-water-demand crops in plots with dry soil profiles, improving stubble balance and soil structure.

 Certainty before sowing: We replace intuition with satellite evidence and traceable agronomic criteria, lowering the financial risk of each season.

Precision intelligence without barriers: We bring cutting-edge technology to producers and technicians who do not have their own weather stations or sensors, without needing hardware investment.

Real support and time savings: Unlike tools that display isolated data without applied criteria, Rotaterra guides every recommendation, saves you hours of technical analysis, and delivers key information about your plot that currently lacks clear access.

What do you hope to achieve?

With Rotaterra, we hope to position crop rotation as a key sustainability practice, demonstrating that it is possible to transform the planning of dominant extensive crops and achieve highly resilient systems simply by intelligently organizing what the market already demands. We seek to reduce the technological gap in agriculture by translating the excess of scattered satellite data into real support, bringing NASA Earth observations closer to producers and advisors without requiring hardware investments. Ultimately, we aspire to contribute to yield stability and agricultural soil conservation, helping the producer stop guessing in the face of increasingly extreme climate scenarios to produce profitably and sustainably.

What tools, programming languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

• Languages: Python 3.11 (server, satellite connection, and agronomic engine) and JavaScript, HTML, and CSS (interface).

• Server (backend): FastAPI with Uvicorn and Pydantic v2; SQLAlchemy 2.0 over SQLite (supports PostgreSQL); login with JWT and passwords encrypted with bcrypt; Farmer, Agricultural Technician, and Administrator profiles.

• Satellite and geospatial data: httpx, NumPy, Shapely, Rasterio, h5py, pyhdf, and pystac-client to read NASA formats (OPeNDAP, HDF/NetCDF, GeoTIFF, and STAC catalogs), with a NASA Earthdata Login account. Each source responds with the same format (common contract) and has automatic fallbacks.

• Interface (frontend): Tailwind CSS, Leaflet 1.9.4 with Leaflet-Geoman 2.17 to draw the plot on the map, Chart.js for up to 5-year time series, and html2pdf.js for the PDF report. In Spanish and English.

• Testing: pytest, 1,116 passing automated tests (run on 11/15/2026 on the latest commit of the rotaterra-completo branch), and GitHub Actions to test each satellite against the real source (results in docs/satelites/).

• Development and deployment: Git and GitHub (one branch and one pull request per satellite), Render (free web service “earth2worlds”, configured with render.yaml), and AI coding assistants: Claude Code and Google Antigravity (see item 6).

• Work methodology: Specification-Driven Development (SDD): each component has its specification in docs/specs/ with objective, rules, and acceptance criteria. Prior research and design; code written and uploaded during the event (11/14 and 11/15/2026).

• Hardware: None specific. There are no sensors or stations in the field: only personal computers and the cloud server.

• Code (GitHub, public): https://github.com/Emmanuel-Funes/Earth2Worlds

Why is the project creative?

Rotaterra is creative because it breaks away from the paradigm of traditional viewers that only display raw data, transforming NASA satellite data into traceable agronomic decisions through an architecture of common contracts and networked satellite connectors. This innovation materializes in a dual interface that democratizes access by adapting both to the producer, with a three-step guided wizard, zero cost, and no need for field sensors, and to the agricultural technician, through an advanced explorer of historical series and editable thresholds. Furthermore, its lightweight architecture avoids the energy consumption of heavy models, optimizing resources through on-demand queries.

This disruptive proposal comes to life thanks to the collaborative work of an interdisciplinary team where each profile contributes indispensable value: Alicia Cendoya (Agronomist) and Leandro J. Rodríguez (B.Sc. in Environmental Management) structure the productive logic and resource sustainability; Emmanuel Funes (Analyst/Programmer) and Hernán Firmapaz (Programmer/Graphic Editor) develop the digital architecture and translate technical complexity into an agile visual interface; and Alfredo Flores (Technical High School Teacher) provides the pedagogical perspective to ensure the tool is truly accessible and practical for any user.
